title: Reading the Law
summary: What the Torah is, how case law and command work, the covenant setting that frames the laws, the older law codes of the ancient Near East and how Israel's laws compare, and the main ways Jews and Christians have related the Law to life and to Christ.

sections.body:
When the Bible speaks of ‘the Law’ it usually means the five books of Moses, Genesis through Deuteronomy, which Jews call the Torah. The Hebrew word torah means instruction or teaching more than statute; a parent's advice in Proverbs is also torah. The name is a reminder that the laws of the Bible sit inside a story. Genesis contains almost no law. Exodus gives nineteen chapters of rescue before the first commandment, and the Ten Commandments themselves begin not with a demand but with a reminder of what God has done: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.” (Exodus 20:2). Law follows grace in the order of the text. Israel is not told to obey in order to be rescued; it is told to live as a people already rescued.

The laws cluster in several collections, each with its own setting and style. Readers new to the Bible often stall in Leviticus because they expect a story and find a manual. It helps to know which collection one is in and what it was for.

Jewish tradition counts 613 commandments in the Torah. The number is attributed in the Babylonian Talmud (Makkot 23b) to Rabbi Simlai, who divided them into 248 positive commands and 365 prohibitions, and the medieval scholar Moses Maimonides listed them one by one in his Book of the Commandments (Sefer HaMitzvot) in the twelfth century. Many of the commands could only be kept in the land, by priests, or while the temple stood; after the temple's destruction in AD 70, rabbinic Judaism carried the law forward through study and interpretation, gathered in the Mishnah (edited about AD 200) and the Talmuds. For Jewish readers the Law has never been a burden to escape but a gift to be studied and loved, as Psalm 119 does at length: “Oh, how I love Your law! All day long it is my meditation.” (Psalm 119:97).

sections.h: Two ways of giving law: command and case
sections.body:
In 1934 the German scholar Albrecht Alt published a study of the origins of Israelite law that drew a distinction still used today. Some laws are apodictic: short, unconditional commands or prohibitions, such as ‘You shall not murder’, with no penalty attached and no exceptions considered. Others are casuistic, or case law: ‘if’ a certain situation arises, ‘then’ this is the ruling. Most of the Book of the Covenant is case law. It begins, “These are the ordinances that you are to set before them” (Exodus 21:1), and proceeds through cases of slavery, assault, injury, theft, and negligence.

The laws about a goring ox show how case law works. “If an ox gores a man or woman to death, the ox must surely be stoned” (Exodus 21:28), and the owner is not held guilty. But if the ox had a habit of goring and the owner had been warned and did nothing, the owner is also liable (21:29), though a ransom may be accepted in place of his life (21:30). The law is not a complete catalogue of every possible ox accident. It sets out representative cases, and a judge was expected to reason from them to cases that were not listed. The difference between the first and second case is the difference between accident and negligence, a principle that applies well beyond oxen.

Deuteronomy's law about roofs works the same way: “If you build a new house, you are to construct a railing around your roof, so that you do not bring bloodguilt on your house if someone falls from it.” (Deuteronomy 22:8). Flat roofs were living space in ancient Israel. The principle is responsibility for the foreseeable danger one's property creates for others, and a modern reader applying it thinks of pool fences and stair rails, not only roofs. Paul reads a law in this spirit when he cites “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain” (Deuteronomy 25:4) and applies it to paying those who preach (1 Corinthians 9:9-10). Interpreters have long differed on whether Paul is reading the law allegorically or drawing out its underlying principle of fair reward for labor, and the answer affects how far his example can be taken as a method.

The apodictic commands, by contrast, state what Israel is as a people. They are addressed to ‘you’ in the singular, to each Israelite, and they draw boundaries rather than resolving disputes. Alt thought the apodictic form was distinctively Israelite and the casuistic form borrowed from the surrounding culture. Later scholars have qualified this, since command forms also appear outside Israel, but the distinction remains a useful tool for reading.

sections.h: The ancient law codes around Israel
sections.body:
Israel was not the first people to write down laws. Since the late nineteenth century archaeologists have recovered a series of law collections from Mesopotamia and Asia Minor, several of them centuries older than Moses on any dating. They are gathered in English in Martha Roth's Law Collections from Mesopotamia and Asia Minor (1995), and they are essential background for reading the laws of the Pentateuch.

The most famous is the collection of Hammurabi, king of Babylon (reigned about 1792 to 1750 BC on the most widely used chronology). It is carved on a black stone pillar about 2.25 meters (7 feet) tall, topped by a relief of the king standing before the sun god Shamash, the god of justice. A French expedition found it in 1901 at Susa in Iran, where an Elamite king had carried it as plunder in the twelfth century BC; it is now in the Louvre in Paris. It contains about 282 laws, framed by a prologue and an epilogue in which Hammurabi presents himself as the king the gods appointed to make justice visible in the land and to protect the weak from the strong.

The collections share a form (prologue, laws, epilogue in the Mesopotamian ones) and much content with the case laws of the Pentateuch: rules for injuries, loans, slaves, marriage, theft, deposits, and damage by animals. The goring ox appears in the Laws of Eshnunna (sections 53 to 55) and the Laws of Hammurabi (sections 250 to 252), with the same distinction as Exodus 21 between an ox with no history and one whose owner had been warned. The principle of ‘eye for eye’ (lex talionis) appears in Hammurabi (sections 196 to 200). Such overlaps show that Israel's case law belonged to a shared legal culture of the ancient Near East. This does not settle how the biblical laws were composed, but it rules out the idea that they fell out of the sky with no connection to the world in which Israel lived.

Scholars also debate what these collections were for. Many Assyriologists, among them F. R. Kraus and Jean Bottéro, noted that the thousands of surviving Mesopotamian court records almost never cite Hammurabi's laws. They concluded that the collections were less statute books than royal monuments and scholarly treatises: models of justice, displaying the king's wisdom and teaching judges how to reason. That is a helpful way to think about the biblical case laws too.

sections.h: What is different about Israel's law
sections.body:
Set beside its neighbors, Israel's law shows real family resemblance and some striking differences. Moshe Greenberg, in an influential 1960 essay on the postulates of biblical criminal law, argued that the differences are not random but flow from different convictions about God and human life.

First, the lawgiver is different. Hammurabi's laws are the king's laws; the gods commission him, but the justice is his, and he boasts of it. In the Pentateuch no king makes law at all. God speaks the law directly, and Deuteronomy even requires Israel's future king to copy the law and read it so that he will not think himself above his brothers (Deuteronomy 17:18-20). Law is therefore not the property of the state, and every person, including the king, stands under it.

Second, the setting is different. Mesopotamian collections are legal texts; the Torah mixes civil law, worship, ethics, and story, and mixes them on purpose. In Leviticus 19 a law about harvest gleanings for the poor stands beside the command to love one's neighbor, a law about fair weights, and a prohibition on mixing two kinds of seed. Nothing in life lies outside God's claim. The laws also give reasons and motives, which the Mesopotamian collections almost never do: “You must not exploit or oppress a foreign resident, for you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt.” (Exodus 22:21).

Third, the value placed on human life is different. In Hammurabi, penalties vary by class: injuring a noble brings retaliation in kind, injuring a commoner or a slave brings a fine. Some property crimes carry the death penalty. In the Pentateuch, murder cannot be settled by a payment (Numbers 35:31), while property crimes are punished by restitution, not death. The ox that kills a person is stoned and its meat may not be eaten, which treats the killing of a human being as a violation of the image of God (compare Genesis 9:5-6) rather than a mere loss of property. And the ‘eye for eye’ principle applies equally to all free persons.

Fourth, the concern for the vulnerable is sharper. The Mesopotamian prologues speak of protecting widows and orphans, but Israel's laws build that concern into the economy: gleanings left in the field for the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow (Deuteronomy 24:19); a weekly Sabbath rest that includes slaves and animals; the release of debts and debt slaves every seventh year; and the return of land in the Jubilee (Leviticus 25). Even an enemy's stray animal must be returned (Exodus 23:4). The laws do not abolish every institution of their world, including slavery and the unequal status of women, and a later section takes up that difficulty, but they press against the grain of that world in a consistent direction.

sections.h: Covenant: the frame around the laws
sections.body:
The laws of the Pentateuch are not free-standing; they are the terms of a covenant, a binding relationship between God and Israel sealed at Sinai. Before the Ten Commandments, God says: “You have seen for yourselves what I did to Egypt, and how I carried you on eagles’ wings and brought you to Myself.” (Exodus 19:4). The obedience that follows is a response to that act, and the purpose is relational: Israel is to be God's treasured possession, “a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Exodus 19:6). After the Book of the Covenant is read, the people answer, “All that the LORD has spoken we will do, and we will be obedient.” (Exodus 24:7), and the covenant is sealed with sacrifice and a meal.

In 1954 George Mendenhall drew attention to the resemblance between this covenant and the treaties that Hittite great kings made with their vassal kings in the fourteenth and thirteenth centuries BC. Those treaties typically open by naming the great king, then recount the history of his kindness to the vassal, then set out the obligations, then provide for the treaty to be deposited in a temple and read publicly, then list the gods as witnesses, and end with blessings for loyalty and curses for betrayal. Meredith Kline (Treaty of the Great King, 1963) argued that Deuteronomy as a whole follows this pattern, and Kenneth Kitchen argued that the Sinai covenant matches the late second millennium form in particular. Other scholars, notably Moshe Weinfeld (Deuteronomy and the Deuteronomic School, 1972), have stressed the close parallels between Deuteronomy's curses and the Neo-Assyrian treaties of Esarhaddon from 672 BC, and date Deuteronomy's composition accordingly to the seventh century. The dating debate is real; the basic point, that the laws are covenant stipulations set within a history of grace and followed by blessings and curses, is shared by both sides.

This frame changes how the laws read. They are not a ladder by which Israel climbs into God's favor. Deuteronomy insists that God chose Israel not because it was numerous or good, but “because the LORD loved you and kept the oath He swore to your fathers” (Deuteronomy 7:8). Nor are they impossible: “this commandment I give you today is not too difficult for you or beyond your reach” (Deuteronomy 30:11). The law included provision for failure, in the sacrifices and the Day of Atonement, because the covenant assumed a people who would sin and need forgiveness. The whole shape of the law, with its sanctuary at the center, is about how a holy God can live among a sinful people.

sections.h: The Ten Commandments and their numbering
sections.body:
The Ten Commandments appear twice, in Exodus 20 and Deuteronomy 5, with small differences. The most notable is the reason for the Sabbath: in Exodus it looks back to God's rest after creation, in Deuteronomy to Israel's release from slavery in Egypt, so that servants and animals too must rest. The Bible calls them ‘the ten words’ (Exodus 34:28; Deuteronomy 4:13), but it never numbers them, and Jewish and Christian traditions divide the text in different ways. The differences explain why a Catholic or Lutheran catechism and a Reformed or Orthodox one number the same commandments differently.

The Jewish tradition treats the opening declaration, ‘I am the LORD your God, who brought you out’, as the first word, and combines the prohibition of other gods and of images as the second. The division used by Philo and Josephus in the first century, and later by the Orthodox and Reformed churches and the Anglican tradition, makes the prohibition of images a separate second commandment. Augustine, followed by the Catholic Church and by Luther, joins other gods and images into one commandment and then divides the prohibition of coveting into two, following the wording of Deuteronomy 5:21, which separates the neighbor's wife from the neighbor's house and goods.

The difference is not merely one of counting. The Reformed tradition's separate commandment against images was bound up with its opposition to images in worship, while Catholic and Lutheran practice read the prohibition as aimed at idols. Each tradition has good ancient precedent for its division.

sections.h: Reading the laws that trouble modern readers
sections.body:
Some laws are hard for modern readers: the death penalty for Sabbath-breaking and certain sexual offenses, laws regulating slavery, laws in which women appear under the authority of fathers and husbands, and the laws of warfare. Critics since the Enlightenment have pointed to these as evidence that the Torah's morality is simply that of its time. The difficulty should be stated plainly, and several considerations, each defended by serious interpreters, bear on it.

The first is that many laws regulate rather than endorse. Jesus says of the divorce law in Deuteronomy 24: “Moses wrote this commandment for you because of your hardness of heart.” (Mark 10:5), and points back to creation as God's intention. A law can limit a harm in a fallen society without declaring the harm good. Many interpreters, such as Christopher Wright (Old Testament Ethics for the People of God, 2004) and Paul Copan (Is God a Moral Monster?, 2011), read the slavery laws in this light: most of what the Pentateuch calls slavery was debt servitude, limited to six years for a fellow Israelite (Exodus 21:2), with protections unknown elsewhere, including freedom for a slave whose master knocks out an eye or a tooth (Exodus 21:26-27) and a prohibition on returning an escaped slave (Deuteronomy 23:15-16). Critics reply that the laws still permitted lifelong ownership of foreigners (Leviticus 25:44-46), and that this cannot be explained away. Both observations are true to the text.

The second is that ‘eye for eye’ was a limit, not a license. It restrained vengeance to what fits the injury, and it put punishment in the hands of courts rather than families. Jewish tradition, in the Mishnah (Bava Kamma 8:1) and the Talmud, interpreted it as requiring monetary compensation equal to the injury, and the law about the slave's eye already implies that literal retaliation was not the only way it was applied. When Jesus says “You have heard that it was said, ‘Eye for eye and tooth for tooth.’” (Matthew 5:38) and calls his followers not to retaliate, he addresses personal revenge, not the justice of courts.

The third is that the Old Testament itself shows the law as a stage in a longer story, looking beyond itself. The prophets promise a day when God will write his law on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33). Christians read the whole Torah in the light of that promise and its fulfillment, which is the subject of the next section. None of these points makes every difficulty disappear, and honest readers across traditions admit as much.

sections.h: Christ and the Law: how Christians have read it
sections.body:
The New Testament holds two sets of statements together. Jesus says, “Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets. I have not come to abolish them, but to fulfill them.” (Matthew 5:17). Paul says “the law is holy, and the commandment is holy, righteous, and good” (Romans 7:12) and that faith does not nullify the law but upholds it (Romans 3:31). Yet Mark comments that Jesus' teaching declared “all foods are clean” (Mark 7:19), the Jerusalem council of about AD 49 declined to require circumcision of Gentile believers (Acts 15), Hebrews calls the law “only a shadow of the good things to come” (Hebrews 10:1), and Paul writes that “Christ is the end of the law” (Romans 10:4), where the Greek telos can mean goal or termination, and commentators divide over which is meant or whether both are. Every Christian tradition has had to explain how these fit.

The early church rejected the answer of Marcion, who about AD 144 taught that the God of the Law was a lesser god than the Father of Jesus and cut the Old Testament from his Bible. Against him, writers such as Irenaeus insisted that one God gave both covenants, the first preparing for the second. From the patristic period onward, and in developed form in Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae, part I-II, questions 98 to 105), Christians commonly divided the Mosaic law into moral laws (such as the Ten Commandments, still binding because they express God's character), ceremonial laws (sacrifices, food laws, festivals, fulfilled in Christ and no longer practiced), and judicial or civil laws (Israel's state law, expired with that state though their general equity remains instructive). Calvin (Institutes 4.20.14-16) and the Westminster Confession of Faith (1646, chapter 19) adopted this threefold division, and it remains the most widely used framework among Protestants and Catholics.

Lutheran theology stresses the distinction between law and gospel: the law commands and accuses, the gospel gives and forgives, and confusing them corrupts both. Lutheran and Reformed theologians alike spoke of three uses of the law: restraining evil in society, showing sinners their need of grace, and guiding believers in grateful obedience. The Formula of Concord (1577) affirmed the third use, and Calvin (Institutes 2.7.12) called it the principal use, while Lutherans have typically given the second use the greatest weight.

Other Protestant traditions draw the lines differently. Dispensationalists and advocates of what is called New Covenant Theology hold that the Mosaic covenant as a whole ended with Christ, and that believers are under ‘the law of Christ’, which restates much of the moral law in new form. At the other end, the theonomy movement of R. J. Rushdoony (The Institutes of Biblical Law, 1973) and Greg Bahnsen (Theonomy in Christian Ethics, 1977) argued that the judicial laws, penalties included, still bind civil governments; most Reformed churches have rejected that position. Since the 1970s the so-called New Perspective on Paul, associated with E. P. Sanders (Paul and Palestinian Judaism, 1977), James Dunn, and N. T. Wright, has argued that first-century Judaism was not a religion of earning salvation by works and that Paul's quarrel was with the law as a boundary marking Jew from Gentile; critics such as Stephen Westerholm and D. A. Carson have defended the Reformation reading of Paul in response.

Amid these differences there is broad agreement on some things. Jesus summarized the whole law in two commands drawn from it, to love God with all the heart (Deuteronomy 6:5) and the neighbor as oneself (Leviticus 19:18), and said “All the Law and the Prophets hang on these two commandments.” (Matthew 22:40). Paul says the same: “love is the fulfillment of the law” (Romans 13:10). For Christians, then, reading the Law means asking what each law showed about God's holiness and his care for people, how Christ fulfills it, and how its underlying concern takes shape in a life of love. A law about roof railings, gleaning, or an ox's muzzle may not be obeyed as written by a Christian today, but it still teaches.
